title: Two Earths Under One Sun: How Ice Can Lock In a Climate

source.title: Entropy production and multiple equilibria: the case of the ice-albedo feedback
source.authors: C. Herbert, D. Paillard, and B. Dubrulle

intro.summary: This lesson draws on four sources and asks one question: how can ice, which reflects sunlight, give a planet more than one possible climate? Its core is Herbert, Paillard and Dubrulle (2011). They used a very simple whole-Earth energy balance model in which shiny ice appears as the planet cools. They found that for sunlight between about 0.98 and 1.08 times today's value, the model has three balanced climates: a frozen snowball, a warm ice-free state like today's, and an unstable state in between. Which climate the planet ends up in depends on its history. Two Wikipedia articles (on ice–albedo feedback and on Snowball Earth) add the observed and geological context. Von Paris et al. (2013) show that the feedback is much weaker for planets around red dwarf (M) stars and under thick atmospheres. Main limitation: the core model is a deliberately crude teaching-scale model with one temperature for the whole planet, so its tipping-point numbers are not predictions for the real Earth. Whether Earth was ever fully frozen is still debated, since a 'slushball' with open tropical water is also possible. Gaps you can follow up later: the paper's own new idea (choosing heat flows by 'maximum entropy production', MEP), how star type and atmosphere weaken the feedback, Arctic amplification today, and the geological evidence for and against Snowball Earth.
background: Sunlight is the planet's income of energy, and the heat it radiates back to space is its spending; temperature settles where the two match.
Albedo is the share of incoming sunlight a surface reflects: fresh snow reflects most of it, while dark ocean absorbs almost all of it.
A feedback is a loop in which a change causes effects that come back to change the original thing again, making it bigger (positive) or smaller (negative).
In 1969 Mikhail Budyko and William Sellers independently built the first simple climate models showing that ice reflectivity could make climate very sensitive.
intro.aha: Under exactly the same sunlight, the same planet can be frozen solid or comfortably warm, and only its past decides which; once it is frozen, sunlight must rise well above today's level to thaw it.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Ice is white and open sea is dark, so ice sends far more sunlight back to space. If the planet warms a little, some ice melts. Dark sea is exposed, more sunlight is absorbed, and the planet warms further. The same loop works in reverse when the planet cools. Scientists have asked since the 1960s whether this loop could make the climate jump between very different states.
primer.quote: Indeed, the higher the global temperature on Earth, the less the ice cover is likely to extend, and thus the lower the albedo. A lower albedo leads in turn to a higher global temperature, and so on and so forth until all the ice is melted.

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: Herbert and colleagues treated the whole Earth as just two boxes: one for the ground and one for the air above it. They let the planet's reflectivity switch smoothly from 'icy' to 'ice-free' around the freezing point. Then they searched for every temperature at which incoming sunlight exactly balances outgoing heat, and tested whether each balance point holds or falls apart. They repeated this for many strengths of sunlight. They also compared this standard approach with a newer idea, the maximum entropy production principle (MEP). Separately, von Paris and colleagues calculated how much light icy and ice-free planets reflect around a Sun-like star and around a red dwarf, using many different atmospheres.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: With a fixed reflectivity there is only one balanced climate, near 288 K (about 15 °C). Once ice is allowed to brighten the planet as it cools, today's sunlight allows three balance points: a snowball near 249 K, an ice-free climate near 287 K, and an in-between state near 275 K. The two outer states hold firm when nudged. The middle one tips towards one or the other at the slightest nudge. Between about 0.98 and 1.08 times today's sunlight, the planet's past decides which climate it is in. The MEP approach found matching balance points, but it needed an extra rule in time to tell stable from unstable.
primer.quote: For example, the temperature and the ice cover of the planet are linked in a positive feedback which gives birth to multiple equilibria for some values of the solar constant: fully ice-covered Earth, ice-free Earth and an intermediate unstable solution.

primer.heading: Why it matters and its limits
primer.body: This loop is a leading explanation for Snowball Earth, the hypothesis that the planet froze over about 700 million years ago. It also explains why escaping a snowball would need an enormous build-up of volcanic CO2. Today the loop helps the Arctic warm nearly four times faster than the globe as a whole. The geology is still disputed, though, and the model is a deliberately crude cartoon. Von Paris and colleagues add that the feedback depends on the star and the air: red dwarf starlight falls mostly at colours where ice is dark, and thick atmospheres hide the surface.
primer.quote: Several unanswered questions remain, including whether Earth was a full "snowball" or a "slushball" with a thin equatorial band of open (or seasonally open) water.

primer.heading: Not every planet feels it equally
primer.body: The same ice can matter much less on other worlds. Von Paris and colleagues calculated how much light planets reflect around a Sun-like star and around a red dwarf, using different atmospheres. Around red dwarfs, and under thick CO2 air, covering a planet in ice barely changes how much light it reflects. That weakens the loop.
primer.quote: At high CO2 pressures, the ice-albedo feedback is strongly reduced for planets around M stars.

concepts.title: Shiny ice, dark sea: how much sunlight bounces back
concepts.idea: The more of a planet's surface is covered by ice, the larger the share of sunlight it reflects, and the less it absorbs.

predict.question: In summer, a large patch of Arctic sea ice melts and leaves dark open water. The same sunlight still arrives there. What happens to the sunlight that patch absorbs?
options: It goes up: open water keeps much more of the same sunlight than ice did
It goes down: water is wet and shiny, so it reflects more than ice
It stays the same, because the sunlight arriving has not changed
It goes down, because less sunlight reaches a melting region
why: Right. Ice sent much of the light back to space. Dark water sends back only about 5% and keeps the rest, so the patch absorbs more and warms.
Water can glint at a low Sun, but on average open sea is one of the darkest surfaces on Earth. In the model it bounces back only 5%, far less than ice.
The light arriving is fixed, but the split is not. What the surface is made of decides how much of that same light is kept and how much is sent back.
Melting does not dim the Sun. The arriving bar stayed at 340 the whole time; only the split between reflected and absorbed changed.

terms.means: The share of arriving sunlight that the ground or sea itself bounces back, from 0 (keeps everything) to 1 (bounces everything)
Soot, dust or algae making snow and ice darker, so it reflects less and absorbs more

model.title: Where the sunlight goes: bounced back or soaked up
model.note: Teaching model: the planet is one flat surface split into ice and open sea. It has no air, clouds or seasons, and every patch gets the same light. The 340 W/m² of arriving sunlight is the global-average figure von Paris et al. use (s4). Open sea bouncing back 5% matches the ocean value they cite (s4). Ice shine is yours to set; they report fresh snow near 0.9 in visible light. The resulting numbers are illustrative, not any paper's results. In a real planet, air and clouds also reflect and absorb, which s4 shows can weaken the effect of ice.

controls.label: How shiny the ice is (share it bounces back)

steps.say: Sunlight pours onto a planet: about 340 watts on every square metre, like a few bright light bulbs shining on each square metre of ground.
Some of that light bounces straight back out to space.
The rest soaks in and warms the planet.
This slider sets how much of the surface is ice. Everything else is dark open sea. Watch the bars as it moves.
This one sets how shiny the ice itself is. Fresh snow is bright; dusty or dirty ice is duller.

explore.prompt: Now you are in charge of the planet's surface. Freeze it, melt it, dirty it, and watch where the sunlight goes.

goals.text: Without changing how shiny the ice is, make the planet soak up less than 200 W/m² of sunlight
hints: Which slider swaps dark sea for bright ice?
Each extra slice of ice swaps a patch that keeps nearly everything for one that sends much of the light back. Watch the soaked-up bar fall as you add ice.
A little ice is not enough. You will need well over half of the planet frozen.

goals.text: Keep at least half of the planet frozen, yet make it soak up more than 250 W/m²
hints: Half ice normally sends a lot of light back. Besides how much ice there is, what else decides how much bounces?
Make the ice itself darker, as if it were dusted with soot or tinted by algae.
Keep the ice at half and lower the shine one step at a time until the soaked-up bar climbs past 250.

feedback.correct: Yes. The sunlight arriving stays the same, but swapping bright ice for dark water changes how it is split. Much more is kept, so the region gains heat.
feedback.incorrect: It is tempting to think the surface does not matter if the same light arrives. But the light is split between bounced back and soaked up, and what the surface is made of sets that split. Ice sends much of it back; open sea keeps about 95%.

steps.say: Start with no ice at all: a planet of open sea. Dark water bounces back only 5%, so about 323 of the 340 W/m² soak in.
That share bounced back is the planet's albedo (its reflectivity, from 0 to 1). Here we count only the ground and sea, so we call it the surface albedo: 5%.
Now freeze 30% of the surface. Each ice patch bounces back 60% instead of 5%. The bounced-back bar grows and the soaked-up bar shrinks.
Go to 60% ice. Every extra 10% of ice turns away about 19 more W/m². The change is steady: same step in ice, same step in light.
The ice's own brightness matters too. Dull it, the way soot or algae do, and the same ice cover soaks up much more. This is snow darkening.
Back to clean ice, and freeze the whole planet. The same Sun shines, yet only 136 W/m² soak in, less than half of what the ice-free planet kept.

understand.explanation: Every surface splits the sunlight it receives into two parts: some bounces back to space and the rest is soaked up as heat. Ice and snow are bright, so they send back a large share, while open sea is dark and keeps almost all of it. So the more of a planet is iced over, the higher its surface albedo and the less sunlight it absorbs, even though the same light arrives. Dirty ice reflects less than clean snow, so how bright the ice is also matters. Herbert et al. (s3) build exactly this into their climate model, letting the planet's albedo rise from an ice-free value to an icy one. Von Paris et al. (s4) add a caution: in a planet with a thick atmosphere or clouds, the air reflects and absorbs too, so the ice's effect on the total can shrink a lot.
understand.quote: Because ice is very reflective, it reflects far more solar energy back to space than open water or any other land cover.

connect.caption: Eq. 1 of Herbert et al. (s3). Ψ^{SW}_{gs} (the soaked-up bar) is sunlight absorbed by the ground. α (the bounced-back share) is the surface albedo. ξS is the average sunlight arriving, about 342 W/m² with their values, near our 340. (s̄ − s) is the share passing their atmosphere; our airless model sets it to 1. Our rule: absorbed = 340 × (1 − α), with α = 0.05 × sea share + ice shine × ice share. More ice gives a bigger α and less absorbed.

concepts.recap: Ice turns sunlight away and dark sea keeps it, so more ice means a higher albedo and less absorbed sunlight from the same Sun.

concepts.title: Where sunlight in meets heat out
concepts.idea: A planet settles at the one temperature where the sunlight it absorbs equals the heat it radiates away, which rises steeply with temperature.

terms.means: The temperature where energy coming in equals energy going out, so the planet stops warming or cooling
The rule that the heat a body radiates grows with the fourth power of its temperature: double the temperature (in kelvin) and it sheds 16 times as much
How strong sunlight is where the planet orbits; the paper uses 1368 W/m² for today's Earth
A simple climate model that only tracks energy coming in and energy going out

model.title: Sunlight in and heat out at each temperature
model.note: Teaching model: one surface layer with a reflectivity that does not change with temperature. The paper's model has a separate atmosphere layer. Here the greenhouse effect and that layer are folded into one constant: heat out = 0.745 × σT⁴. The constant was chosen so that today's Sun (1368 W/m², multiplied by the paper's factor 0.25) and reflectivity 0.15 give the paper's 288 K. All other numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

y.label: Energy per square metre each second (W/m²)

steps.say: This picture tracks a planet's energy. Left to right is temperature in kelvin, where 273 is freezing. Up is energy per square metre, each second.
The flat line is the sunlight the planet soaks up. It is the same at every temperature.
The rising curve is the heat the planet glows away. A warmer planet sheds much more.
This slider sets how strong the Sun is compared with today. Watch the flat line rise.
This one sets reflectivity, the share of sunlight bounced straight back. More bounce means a lower flat line.
And this test temperature lets you check any temperature you like.

explore.prompt: You control the Sun and the planet's shine. Move the crossing point to where you want the planet to live.

goals.text: Keep today's Sun, and make the planet settle right at freezing (within 1 K of 273 K).
hints: Freezing is colder than today's 288 K. Should the planet soak up more sunlight or less?
Raise the reflectivity, as if you added snow or clouds, and watch the Balance line slide left.
You need roughly twice today's reflectivity. Fine-tune until the balance reads 273 K.

goals.text: Brighten the Sun by at least 5%, then bring the planet back to within 1 K of today's 288 K.
hints: A brighter Sun lifts the flat line. Which other slider can push it back down?
Turn up the Sun first, then raise the reflectivity until the crossing returns to 288 K.
Each 5% of extra sunlight needs only a few hundredths of extra reflectivity to cancel it.

predict.question: Picture the same planet at 288 K. Now the sunlight it absorbs doubles, and the way it sheds heat stays the same. Where does it settle?
options: About 576 K: twice as hot
About 340 K: roughly a fifth hotter
Still 288 K
It keeps heating forever
why: Doubling the input makes doubling the temperature feel natural. But heat out grows with the fourth power of temperature, so twice the heat out needs only about 1.19 times the temperature.
Right. Heat out must double to match the new input, and that takes a temperature 2^(1/4) ≈ 1.19 times higher: 288 × 1.19 ≈ 342 K.
This would only hold if heat out could rise without the temperature changing. The planet has to warm until it glows away the extra energy.
The heat-out curve keeps climbing, so it always catches up with a higher flat line. There is still exactly one crossing, just further right.

feedback.correct: Yes. The planet warms until it sheds the doubled input. Because heat out rises with temperature to the fourth power, that happens at only about 1.19 × 288 ≈ 342 K.
feedback.incorrect: The planet always moves to where heat out equals sunlight in. Heat out climbs so steeply with temperature that doubling the input raises the temperature by only about a fifth, to roughly 342 K.

steps.say: Put the planet at 240 K, well below freezing. It soaks up about 291 W/m² but glows away only about 140.
So it gains about 150 W/m² of net heating. More comes in than goes out, and the planet warms.
At 270 K it still gains, about 66 W/m², but less than before. The heat-out curve has climbed toward the flat line.
Overshoot to 310 K and the sign flips. It loses about 99 W/m² more than it gets, so it cools back down.
Only near 288 K does heat out match sunlight in. Net heating is zero and the temperature stops changing. This is the equilibrium temperature.

Why only one crossing? The flat line ignores temperature, and heat out rises faster and faster, with temperature to the fourth power. That rule is the Stefan–Boltzmann law. A flat line and an ever-rising curve can meet only once.
Today's sunlight strength is the solar constant, 1368 W/m² in the paper. Raise it 15%: the crossing slides to about 298 K. That is only 3.5% warmer, because the steep curve soaks up most of the push.

Now keep today's Sun but bounce back 60% of the light, like a mostly icy planet. The crossing drops to about 239 K, a deep freeze. Tracking only energy in and out like this is called an energy balance model.

understand.explanation: Sunlight brings energy in, and the planet sheds energy as heat. Below the crossing it gains more than it loses and warms; above the crossing it loses more and cools. So it settles where the two are equal. Heat out rises steeply with temperature, roughly as its fourth power. With reflectivity held fixed, the flat sunlight line can cross that curve only once, giving one balance temperature. Herbert and colleagues built a small energy balance model with a ground layer and an atmosphere layer. With reflectivity fixed at 0.15, they found exactly one balance point, near 288 K, close to Earth's average. Our model squeezes their atmosphere and greenhouse effect into one constant, so only the 1368 W/m², the 0.15 and the 288 K come from the paper.
understand.quote: Taking for the albedo the ﬁxed value α0 = 0.15, the system only has one ﬁxed point

connect.caption: This is the teaching model's rule, a simplified version of the paper's. Sunlight in (left) uses the paper's form: reflectivity α, the factor ξ = 0.25 that spreads sunlight over the globe, and sunlight strength S, today 1368 W/m². Heat out (right) is σT⁴, with σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ W/m²/K⁴. The constant k = 0.745 stands in for the paper's greenhouse and atmosphere terms. Where the two sides are equal, T is the balance temperature.

concepts.recap: A planet warms or cools until the heat it radiates equals the sunlight it absorbs. Because heat out climbs so steeply, with fixed reflectivity there is just one such temperature.

activities.title: A planet that starts too cold

steps.text: Today's Sun, reflectivity 0.15: the planet soaks up about 291 W/m². It starts at 250 K and glows away about 165.
It has warmed to 270 K. Heat out has risen to about 224 W/m².
steps.result: Net heating ≈ +66 W/m²: still warming, but more slowly

steps.text: At 285 K, heat out is about 279 W/m².
At 288 K, heat out is about 291 W/m², the same as sunlight in.
steps.result: Net heating ≈ 0: the temperature stops changing

activities.takeaway: The gap between in and out shrinks as the planet warms, so it closes in on the crossing and stays there. A planet starting too hot would slide down to the same point.

concepts.title: The loop: melt, darken, warm, melt again
concepts.idea: Because a warmer planet has less ice and so absorbs more sunlight, a small warming triggers extra warming, and each round of the loop adds to the last.

predict.question: Imagine a planet whose loop is much stronger than any setting on the slider: each round hands back 99% of the last round's warming. A small first push of warming starts the loop. What happens to the total warming?
options: It settles at about twice the first push
It becomes enormous, because each round adds almost as much as the one before
It stays equal to the first push
It turns into cooling once the ice is gone
why: Twice the push is what a loop strength of one half gives. At 0.99 the rounds hardly shrink, so the sum keeps climbing far past double.

Right. Each round is 99% of the last, so the sum works out to about 100 times the push. On a real planet the runaway stops only when the ice runs out, as the paper says: 'until all the ice is melted'.
The total equals the push only when the loop is cut, for example when the ice is held fixed. A loop that hands back 99% each round adds a great deal.
Losing ice makes the planet darker, so it absorbs more sunlight, not less. When the ice is gone the loop simply has nothing left to melt. It does not reverse into cooling.

terms.means: The loop in which warming melts ice, the darker surface absorbs more sunlight, and that warms the planet further (it also runs in reverse: cooling grows ice, which cools more)
The share of each round's warming that the loop hands back as fresh warming in the next round
How many times bigger the total warming ends up than the first push

model.title: A loop of causes: warmth, ice and sunlight
model.note: Teaching model: the whole loop is squeezed into one number, the share of each round's warming handed back in the next round, and that share is held constant. On a real planet the ice response changes with season, place and how much ice is left, and the loop stops once the ice is gone. All numbers are illustrative, not data from the sources.

controls.label: Loop strength (share handed back each round)

outputs.label: Total warming once the loop settles
Times bigger than the first push

steps.say: This is a loop of causes. It starts on the left with a first push of warming, which could come from anything.
Follow the arrows. A warmer planet has less ice. Less ice bounces less sunlight away, so more is soaked up, and that warms the planet again.
This slider sets the size of the first push.
This slider sets the loop strength: how much of each round's warming comes back as new warming. Watch the 'warmer → less ice' arrow thicken.
This switch holds the ice fixed, so warming can't melt it. That cuts the loop.

explore.prompt: Play with the push, the loop strength and the ice switch. Find settings where the loop does most of the work, then see what it takes to warm the planet with the loop cut.

goals.text: Make the loop more than double the first push, while the total warming stays below 1.5 °C
hints: Two things set the total: how big the push is and how strong the loop is. Only one of them sets the 'times bigger' number.
The 'times bigger' number depends only on loop strength. Raise it until that number passes 2, then check that the total is still below 1.5 °C.
The multiplier passes 2 once more than half of each round comes back. Go a little past one half and leave the push small.

goals.text: Hold the ice fixed, and still reach at least the total warming that a 0.5 °C push gives when the loop hands back 60% each round
hints: First work out the target: what total does a 0.5 °C push reach with the loop at 0.6? You can try it on the model before flipping the switch.
With the ice fixed, rounds 2 and 3 read zero, so the total is just the first push. The loop strength slider no longer matters.
The bare push now has to reach the target by itself. That needs a push more than twice as big as 0.5 °C.

feedback.correct: Yes. Each round hands back a share of the round before. When that share is close to 1, the rounds barely shrink, so the sum grows to many times the push. Only running out of ice can stop it.
feedback.incorrect: The total is the push plus every round the loop adds, and each round is the loop strength times the round before. At a strength of 0.99 the rounds hardly shrink, so the sum becomes about 100 times the push. On a real planet only running out of ice stops it.

steps.say: Start with ice that doesn't respond to temperature: loop strength 0. A 0.5 °C push gives 0.5 °C in total, and nothing more.
Now let the ice respond, with 30% handed back each round. The push melts some ice, the darker surface soaks up more sunlight, and round 2 adds 0.15 °C.
That extra warming melts a little more ice. Round 3 adds 30% of round 2, about 0.045 °C. Each round is smaller than the last, but every one adds to the total.
Add all the rounds and the total settles near 0.71 °C, about 1.4 times the push. This loop, from temperature to ice to reflected light to absorbed light and back, is the ice–albedo feedback.
The loop strength has a name: the feedback factor. Turn it up to 0.6 and each round hands back 60%. The total is now 2.5 times the push. That multiple is the amplification.
At 0.9 the same small push becomes 5 °C, ten times bigger. A stronger loop makes each round add more, and the rounds stay large for longer.

Now hold the ice fixed. The loop is cut and the total falls back to the bare push. Climate modellers run this test: in their models, strong Arctic warming largely disappears when sea ice is held fixed.

understand.explanation: Warming melts ice, which makes the surface darker. A darker surface soaks up more sunlight, which brings more warming and more melting. Each pass round the loop hands back a share of the last round's warming, so a small push ends up as a larger total. A bigger share gives a bigger total. In the 1960s Budyko and Sellers built simple energy-balance models and showed that this loop could have dramatic effects. It also runs in reverse: cooling grows ice, which reflects more light and cools further. Today, climate models that hold sea ice fixed lose most of the extra-fast Arctic warming, which is evidence that the loop is real. One caution: a real feedback factor is not a single fixed number. It changes with season and location, and the loop can only run until the ice is gone.
understand.quote: Indeed, the higher the global temperature on Earth, the less the ice cover is likely to extend, and thus the lower the albedo. A lower albedo leads in turn to a higher global temperature, and so on and so forth until all the ice is melted.

connect.caption: This is the teaching model's own rule, not an equation from the sources. ΔT_{0} (blue) is the first push. g (orange) is the loop strength, or feedback factor. Round 2 adds g × ΔT_{0}, round 3 adds g² × ΔT_{0}, and so on. ΔT_{total} is the settled sum. 1/(1 − g) is the amplification, and it grows without limit as g nears 1. The paper's own models do not use a fixed g. They let reflectivity change smoothly with temperature, which comes next in the lesson.

concepts.recap: Each round of melt, darken, warm hands back a share of the last round's warming. The bigger that share, the more a small push grows.

concepts.title: Let ice switch on: one crossing becomes three
concepts.idea: When reflectivity rises smoothly from 'ice-free' to 'icy' as the planet cools past freezing, the absorbed-sunlight curve bends into an S and can cross the heat-out curve three times.

predict.question: Around a red dwarf star, most starlight arrives at colours that ice reflects poorly. Imagine a planet there whose icy and ice-free reflectivity are close, say 0.30 versus 0.20, instead of 0.68 versus 0.08. With the ice switched on, what happens to the curves?
options: The S becomes gentler, and the curves may cross only once at every starlight strength
The S becomes sharper, giving three crossings for a wider range of starlight
Nothing changes: the number of crossings depends only on how bright the star is
A fourth crossing appears
why: Right. The height of the S's step comes from the gap between icy and ice-free reflectivity. A small gap gives a shallow bend that never climbs faster than the heat-out curve, so there is room for only one crossing.
Someone might think any ice makes the feedback stronger. A smaller brightness difference between ice and open ground means a smaller step, so the S flattens rather than sharpens.
Starlight does shift the S up and down. But three crossings also need the S to be steep enough near freezing, and that steepness depends on how much brighter ice is than open ground.
One smooth step can bend the line into an S with at most three crossings against the steadily rising heat-out curve. A weaker step gives fewer crossings, not more.

terms.means: More than one temperature at which a planet's energy balances, all for the same sunlight
The coldest balance point, where the whole planet is covered in bright ice
The warmest balance point, where the planet has no ice and absorbs the most sunlight

model.title: Sunlight in and heat out at each temperature, with ice that comes and goes
model.note: Teaching model: the same one-layer planet as before (heat out = 0.745 × σT⁴, with the greenhouse effect folded into that constant). New: when ice is switched on, reflectivity follows the paper's smooth rule (its Eq. 18). It is 0.08 when ice-free and 0.68 when icy, changing over about 15 K around freezing (273.15 K). The paper's Table 1 prints these two values under swapped symbols. We follow its Fig. 3, which shows high reflectivity when cold. While ice is on, the reflectivity slider only moves the dashed comparison line. This model has no separate atmosphere layer, so its crossings differ from the paper's. At today's Sun it gives about 226, 283 and 287 K (paper: 249, 275 and 287 K). Its three crossings appear from 1.00× upward and last past 1.2×, whereas the paper finds them only between 0.98× and 1.08×. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: Ice forms when the planet is cold

y.label: Energy per square metre each second (W/m²)

series.label: Sunlight absorbed if reflectivity never changed

steps.say: Same picture as last time. The flat line is sunlight absorbed and the steep curve is heat radiated away. Where they cross, the planet's energy balances.
One new switch: ice that forms when the planet is cold. Flip it on and watch the flat line bend.
Now reflectivity depends on temperature. Slide the test temperature, and this box shows how much sunlight the surface bounces back there.

explore.prompt: The ice is yours to play with. Hunt with the sunlight slider for Suns that give one crossing or three. Then use the test temperature to see where the planet would gain heat.

goals.text: With ice on, dim the Sun only a little, just enough that the warm crossings disappear and a single crossing is left.
hints: Which part of the S has to sink below the heat-out curve for the warm crossings to vanish?
Switch the ice on, then lower the Sun one step at a time and watch the crossings box after each step.
Keep an eye on the S near 285 K. The warm crossings go within a few hundredths of today's Sun.

goals.text: With three crossings showing, put the test temperature between the middle crossing and the warmest one. Check what the net heating says there.
hints: First you need three crossings. Which switch do you need, and which way should the Sun go?
Brighten the Sun a little so the two warm crossings spread apart, then slide the test temperature into the gap between them.
Between those two crossings the S sits above the heat-out curve, so the net heating there should be positive.

feedback.correct: Yes. Three crossings need a bend steep enough to outrun the heat-out curve near freezing. That steepness comes from how much brighter ice is than open ground. Shrink that difference and the S flattens toward a single crossing.
feedback.incorrect: The S's bend comes from the difference between icy and ice-free reflectivity. When ice is barely brighter than open ground, the step is small. The absorbed line then never climbs faster than heat out, so it crosses only once, whatever the star's brightness.

steps.say: Start with ice off. Reflectivity is 0.15 at every temperature, so absorbed sunlight is a flat line. It meets the steep heat-out curve exactly once, near 288 K.
Switch the ice on. A cold, icy planet bounces back about 68% of sunlight, and a warm, ice-free one only 8%. The line sinks on the cold side and rises on the warm side, so it bends into an S.
Probe the cold side. At 240 K the surface reflects about two-thirds of the sunlight, so only a little is absorbed.
Now the warm side. At 300 K reflectivity is about 0.10, so far more sunlight is absorbed.
Around freezing the S climbs about twice as fast as heat out. That steep stretch lets it cut through heat-out more than once. At today's Sun it only just pokes above heat-out near 285 K.
Turn the Sun up slightly. Now the S crosses heat-out three times, near 229, 277 and 295 K: multiple equilibria. The coldest, fully iced, is the snowball state. The warmest is the ice-free state.
Dim the Sun a little instead. The warm part of the S drops below the heat-out curve, and the two warm crossings vanish. Only the snowball crossing is left, near 223 K.
Back to a slightly brighter Sun: three crossings again. Whether a planet has one balance point or three depends on how brightly the Sun shines.

understand.explanation: Ice makes reflectivity depend on temperature: a cold planet is icy and bright, and a warm planet is dark and absorbs more. That bends the absorbed-sunlight line into an S, steepest around freezing, where it climbs faster than the heat-out curve. A steep enough S can cut through heat-out three times, giving three balance temperatures for the same Sun: a frozen snowball, an ice-free warm planet, and one in between. Herbert, Paillard and Dubrulle (2011) put this smooth reflectivity rule into a simple two-layer energy balance model. They found three solutions for sunlight between about 0.98 and 1.08 of today's value: about 249, 275 and 287 K at today's Sun. Outside that range they found only one. Their model treats the whole planet as one temperature, and our one-layer version shifts the exact numbers. The paper also points out that the split into several balance points comes from radiation, not from how the air moves heat around.
understand.quote: For example, the temperature and the ice cover of the planet are linked in a positive feedback which gives birth to multiple equilibria for some values of the solar constant: fully ice-covered Earth, ice-free Earth and an intermediate unstable solution.

connect.caption: The paper's Eq. 18, the rule the ice switch turns on. α(T_{g}) is the reflectivity at surface temperature T_{g}, shown in the 'Reflectivity at test temperature' box. α_{F} = 0.08 is ice-free, α_{I} = 0.68 is icy, T_{0} = 273.15 K is freezing, and ΔT = 15 K sets how gradual the change is. Far below freezing tanh is near +1, giving the icy value. Far above it is near −1, giving the ice-free value. The model uses an equivalent logistic function.

concepts.recap: Ice turns the flat absorbed-sunlight line into an S, and a steep enough S can balance the planet at three temperatures (snowball, ice-free and in between) under the same Sun.

concepts.title: Valleys and hilltops: which balance points hold
concepts.idea: A balance point is stable if a planet nudged slightly warmer cools back to it (and one nudged cooler warms back); the middle point fails this test, so a planet starting near it rolls off to the snowball or the warm state.

predict.question: In the paper's own model at today's Sun, the snowball state is about 249 K, the middle balance point about 275 K and the warm state about 287 K. A planet sits in the snowball. Roughly how big a sudden, one-off warming would send it to the warm state for good?
options: Any warming at all, however small
A bit more than 26 K, enough to get past the middle point
At least 38 K, enough to reach 287 K directly
None: after any one-off warming it drains back to the snowball
why: This treats the snowball like the middle point. The snowball is a valley: after a small push heat out beats sunlight in, and the planet cools back to 249 K.
Correct. Once the planet is past 275 K, sunlight in beats heat out, so it warms the rest of the way to 287 K by itself.
Tempting, since 287 K is the destination. But the push only has to clear the hilltop; beyond it the planet's own net heating carries it to 287 K.

This would hold if the snowball were the only valley. With two valleys, a push past the hilltop lands in the warm one. This is the idealized model only: for the real Snowball Earth, the proposed escape is a slow build-up of volcanic CO₂.

terms.means: A balance point the planet returns to after a small nudge either way, like a marble at the bottom of a bowl
A balance point where any small nudge grows, so the planet moves away from it, like a marble balanced on a hilltop
The paper's landscape picture: a curve built so temperature always moves downhill on it. Valleys are stable balance points and hilltops are unstable ones

model.title: Sunlight in and heat out at each temperature, with ice that comes and goes
model.note: Teaching model: the same one-layer planet as before. Heat out is 0.745 × σT⁴, with the greenhouse effect folded into that constant. With ice on, reflectivity follows the paper's Eq. 18: 0.08 when ice-free and 0.68 when icy, changing around freezing, as in its Fig. 3 (the paper's Table 1 prints these two values under swapped symbols). New here: the test temperature is treated as the planet's starting temperature. 'Where a planet starting here settles' gives the crossing the planet drifts to, following the sign of net heating. It is worked out from the crossings, not by stepping through time, and it assumes nothing else changes. The warm balance point is found numerically, and 'first estimate' is an intermediate step in that calculation. This model has no separate atmosphere layer, so its crossings differ from the paper's. At today's Sun they are about 226, 283 and 287 K here, versus 249, 275 and 287 K in the paper, so here the middle and warm points are only about 4 K apart. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: Ice forms when the planet is cold

outputs.label: Where a planet starting here settles

y.label: Energy per square metre each second (W/m²)

series.label: Sunlight absorbed if reflectivity never changed

steps.say: Same picture as before, with ice switched on. Sunlight absorbed bends into an S and crosses heat out three times.
The test-temperature slider has a new job: it is now where the planet starts. Compare its two dots. If sunlight in is above heat out, the planet warms. If it is below, the planet cools.
The readouts show the net heating at the start, the warm balance point, and where a planet starting here finally settles, also marked on the curve.

explore.prompt: Treat the test temperature as a starting point. Before you trust the readout, compare the two dots: which way will the planet drift, and which valley will catch it?

goals.text: With the Sun a bit brighter than today, start the planet above freezing and still have it end up in the snowball.
hints: Ice must be on for there to be a snowball to fall into. Where is the middle crossing once the Sun is brighter?
Brighten the Sun only a little, then check starts just above the freezing line. Is the heat-out dot still above the sunlight-in dot there?
The middle crossing moves down as the Sun brightens. With a small brightening, it still sits a few kelvin above freezing, so search in that narrow strip.

goals.text: Start the planet below freezing, yet have it end up in the warm state.
hints: At today's Sun the middle crossing is above freezing, so every start below freezing rolls to the snowball. What could move that crossing?
More sunlight lifts the S-shaped curve. Watch where it now crosses heat out in the middle.
Turn the Sun up a lot, then try starts just below the freezing line until sunlight in beats heat out there.

feedback.correct: Right. The snowball is a valley, so small pushes die out. A push that carries the planet past the hilltop at about 275 K is enough, because beyond it sunlight in beats heat out and the planet warms the rest of the way to 287 K by itself.
feedback.incorrect: The answer depends on which side of the hilltop the push leaves the planet. A small push from a valley dies out. But once the planet is past the middle point (about 275 K in the paper's model), its own net heating carries it into the warm valley. It does not need to be pushed all the way to 287 K.

steps.say: Start the planet exactly on the warm crossing, 287 K. Sunlight in and heat out match and net heating is about zero, so it stays put.
Nudge it 5 K warmer. Heat out now sits above sunlight in. Net heating is about −8 W/m², so the planet cools and slides back to 287 K.
Nudge it 2 K cooler instead. Now sunlight in wins by a hair, so the planet warms back to 287 K. A balance point that pulls the planet back from both sides is called a stable equilibrium.
The snowball crossing near 226 K behaves the same way. Start 10 K above it: heat out wins by about 20 W/m², and the planet cools back down. That is another stable equilibrium.
Now try the middle crossing, near 283 K. Start just above it, at 284 K. Sunlight in wins by about 1 W/m², so the planet warms, and keeps warming until it reaches 287 K.
Start just below it, at 282 K. Heat out wins by about 1 W/m², so the planet cools, and keeps cooling, all the way to the snowball near 226 K. Two starts 2 K apart lead to two different worlds.

The middle crossing pushes every nudge away, so no planet stays there: an unstable equilibrium. Picture two valleys, snowball and warm, with a hilltop between. The paper draws this and calls it a potential.

understand.explanation: A crossing only tells you where sunlight in equals heat out; whether the planet stays there depends on what a small nudge does. At the snowball and warm crossings, a slightly warmer planet loses more heat than it gains, and a slightly cooler one gains more than it loses. So it is pulled back: a stable equilibrium, like a marble at the bottom of a bowl. At the middle crossing the imbalance points away on both sides, so any nudge grows and the planet rolls to the snowball or to the warm state. That is an unstable equilibrium, a hilltop. The paper finds this pattern in its two-layer model at today's Sun: the snowball (about 249 K) and warm (about 287 K) states are stable and the intermediate state (about 275 K) is not. It reads this from whether its warming-rate curve slopes down or up at each crossing, and shows it again as a two-valley landscape (a potential). Both the paper's model and ours are highly idealized planets described by a single temperature, so this shows the mechanism, not a forecast for the real Earth.
understand.quote: The stability can also be read directly on Fig.4 for the 1D-reduced system: stable equilibria correspond to roots of the function with negative derivative, while at the unstable equilibrium, the curve crosses the x-axis with an upward slope.

check.task: With ice forming, put the planet at a starting temperature where it is warming at first (sunlight in beats heat out), yet it still ends up in the snowball.
check.hint: Warming at first doesn't decide the ending; which valley you are in does. Look at starts colder than the snowball balance point.
check.misconception: A planet that is heating up right now must be headed for the warm climate. In fact a planet below the snowball point warms only until it reaches the snowball valley floor, and then it stays there.

connect.caption: The paper's Eq. 28 for the ground layer. c_pg is how much heat the surface stores per degree. T_g is surface temperature (the test temperature slider). R_g + γ_g is the net energy the ground gains each second (the net heating readout). In our one-layer model that right side is simply sunlight absorbed minus heat radiated away. Its sign sets the drift: positive warms, negative cools. A balance point is stable where it goes from positive to negative as temperature rises.

concepts.recap: A balance point holds only if nudges die out: the snowball and warm valleys pull the planet back, while the middle hilltop sends it rolling to one side or the other.

activities.title: A marble in the paper's two-valley landscape

steps.text: Picture a marble. In a bowl, a small push and it rolls back to the bottom. On top of an upside-down bowl, the smallest push and it rolls off and never comes back.
The paper turns its warming-rate curve into a landscape V (a potential), built so that temperature always moves downhill on it.
steps.result: Valley floors = stable balance points; hilltops = unstable ones

steps.text: At today's Sun, the paper's landscape has two valleys, near 250 K and 290 K, with a hilltop near 275 K between them (its Fig. 6).
A planet starting at 265 K is on the cold side of the hilltop, so it rolls down into the snowball valley.
A planet starting at 285 K is on the warm side of the hilltop, so it rolls into the warm valley.

activities.takeaway: Where a planet ends depends on which side of the hilltop it starts. The hilltop itself is a balance point no planet can keep.

concepts.title: Same Sun, two Earths: tipping points and getting stuck
concepts.idea: As sunlight is slowly turned down, the warm climate vanishes near 0.98 of today's value and the planet drops to a snowball; to escape, sunlight must rise past about 1.08, so between the two the climate depends on where the planet came from.

predict.question: Two identical planets now get the same sunlight, 1.04 of today's. Planet A froze long ago, and since then its Sun has wandered between 0.95 and 1.06. Planet B has always been warm, and its Sun has wandered between 1.00 and 1.15. What are they like now?
options: A is frozen and B is warm
Both are warm, because 1.04 is brighter than today's Sun
Both are frozen, because they get the same sunlight
Both sit at the in-between balance point
why: Right: A's Sun never climbed past about 1.08, so its snowball never vanished. B's Sun never fell below about 0.98, so its warm climate never vanished. Same Sun, different pasts, different climates.
Tempting if temperature followed sunlight alone. But at 1.04 the snowball still exists as a balance, and A's Sun never rose past about 1.08, the level needed to remove it.
This assumes the same sunlight must give the same climate. Between about 0.98 and 1.08 both climates exist, and B never left the warm one, because its Sun never dropped below the warm climate's edge.
The in-between balance does exist at 1.04, but it is the unsteady one from the last concept: a planet nudged off it rolls away to warm or frozen, so neither planet rests there.

terms.means: A map showing every temperature where a planet can balance, for each amount of sunlight
The sunlight level where one kind of climate stops existing, so the planet must jump to the other
When a system's state depends on its past, so the way down and the way back up follow different paths

model.title: Where the planet settles, for each amount of sunlight
model.note: Teaching model: two smooth curves fitted to the balance temperatures the paper reports for its simple two-layer, zero-dimensional energy-balance model. These are about −24 °C (249 K) frozen and +14 °C (287 K) warm at today's Sun, about −28 °C at 0.95 and +27 °C at 1.1. The warm climate ends near 0.98 and the snowball near 1.08 of today's sunlight. The curve shapes between those points are illustrative, not the paper's exact curves. The unsteady middle balance is left out. The Sun is assumed to change slowly enough that the planet always settles. A trip is one dimming, down to the 'dimmest' value, followed by one brightening to the 'end' value.

controls.label: Dimmest sunlight earlier in the trip (× today's)
Sunlight at the end of the trip (× today's)

outputs.label: Frozen at the end? (1 = yes, 0 = no)
Gap between the warm and frozen climates at this sunlight (0 = only one exists)

steps.say: This picture maps where a planet's temperature settles. Across is the Sun's strength, as a share of today's: 1.00 is today. Up is the temperature in °C.
The dot is our planet at the end of a long, slow trip in sunlight. Right now it sits at today's Sun, warm at about 14 °C.
This slider sets the sunlight at the end of the trip. Watch the dot glide along.
This one sets how far the Sun was dimmed earlier in the trip. At 1.00 it never dimmed at all.
Two dashed lines mark special sunlight levels. You'll soon see what happens at each.

explore.prompt: Plan trips for the planet. Choose how far the Sun dims, then where it ends up. Guess where the dot will land before you look.

goals.text: End the trip under a Sun a little dimmer than today's, with the planet still warm.
hints: Does the warm path stop exactly at today's Sun, or does it reach a bit further left?
Follow the warm path leftward from today. The planet stays warm until it reaches the end of that path.
Keep both the end sunlight and the earlier dimming to the right of the first dashed line.

goals.text: Freeze the planet, then thaw it again using as little sunlight as possible.
hints: First the planet must freeze. How far must the earlier dimming go?
Once it is frozen, raise the end sunlight one step at a time and watch for the dot to jump up.
The jump comes only once you pass the second dashed line. Try the first step beyond it.

feedback.correct: Yes. Between about 0.98 and 1.08 of today's sunlight, both climates exist. A planet keeps the one it already has until its Sun crosses that climate's own edge. A never crossed 1.08 and B never crossed 0.98, so each kept its climate.
feedback.incorrect: You probably assumed one amount of sunlight gives one temperature. Between the two dashed lines that is false: a warm and a frozen balance both exist, and a planet stays in whichever one it is already in until its Sun crosses that climate's edge.

steps.say: Start today: the Sun at 1.00, the planet warm at about 14 °C, sitting on the warm upper path.

These two paths map every temperature the planet can balance at, for each amount of sunlight. Scientists call such a map a bifurcation diagram. On the far left and far right the two paths run together. In between they split.
Now dim the Sun slowly to 0.95. The warm path ends at the first dashed line. Past it, no warm balance exists, so the planet falls to a snowball, about −28 °C. That edge is a tipping point.
Brighten the Sun back to today's 1.00. Does the warmth come back? No. The bright ice reflects so much sunlight that the planet stays frozen, at about −24 °C.
Go brighter than today, to 1.05. Still frozen, about −18 °C. The planet climbs the lower path, not the upper one.
Only past the second dashed line, the other tipping point, does the snowball balance vanish. At 1.12 the planet jumps to warm, about 29 °C. Down one path, back up another: this loop is hysteresis.
Now take a planet whose Sun never dipped. At today's sunlight it is warm, about 14 °C.

Now one whose Sun dipped to 0.95, then came back to today's. Same Sun, same planet, yet frozen at about −24 °C: a 38 °C gap set only by its past. To thaw, sunlight must climb past the second line, well above today's.

understand.explanation: When the Sun dims slowly, the planet follows the warm path until about 0.98 of today's sunlight. There the warm balance disappears, and the planet falls to a snowball. When the Sun brightens again, the planet stays frozen, because its ice reflects so much sunlight. It stays frozen until about 1.08, where the snowball balance disappears and the planet jumps back to warm. Between these two tipping points both climates are possible, and only the planet's past decides which one it has: this is hysteresis. Herbert and colleagues found the two thresholds by tracking every balance point of their simple two-layer, zero-dimensional model as they swept the sunlight. They note the loop keeps the same basic shape even with the greenhouse effect switched off. The exact numbers belong to this idealized model, and later work found the climate less sensitive than the first such models suggested. For the real Snowball Earth episodes, the proposed way out is a slow build-up of volcanic CO2 over millions of years, not a brighter Sun.
understand.quote: Creation of a pair of stable/unstable equilibria at the tipping points 0.98 S0 and 1.08 S0 is called a saddle-node bifurcation. Thus the hysteresis curve obtained for the temperature stems from the bifurcation structure of the dynamical system as two back-to-back saddle-node bifurcations.

check.task: Freeze the planet using the smallest dip below today's Sun that still works, then leave the Sun at exactly today's level.
check.hint: The planet freezes only if the dimming passes the first dashed line. Go just one step past it, then set the end sunlight back to today's.
check.misconception: That a small dip below today's Sun can't matter once the Sun is restored. In fact, once the dip passes the warm climate's edge the planet freezes, and today's sunlight is not enough to undo it.

connect.caption: The paper's ground energy balance (Eq. 9 with Eq. 11). Absorbed sunlight minus heat lost to air and space, plus surface flux γ_g, sums to zero. S is the Sun's strength (the end slider, as a share of S₀ = 1368 W m⁻²). T_g is the settled ground temperature, the dot. α(T_g) is the ice reflectivity, high when frozen. Every T_g solving this is a balance point: between about 0.98 S₀ and 1.08 S₀ there are three, and the past picks which stable one holds.

concepts.recap: Between about 0.98 and 1.08 of today's sunlight, a planet can be warm or frozen. Its past picks which, and a frozen planet needs far more sunlight than today's to thaw.
